evidence.claims: Numeric claims are all backed by results.txt (headline 0.0075/0.21/5.6 and 0.0025/0.035/1.07 %/yr vs F rows 0.007524/0.2073/5.605 and 0.002547/0.03545/1.068; ~5x = 5.25; 18 and 93 years = 100/5.605 and 100/1.068; doubling 1.16-1.28x and 3.1x vs D; 2.4 pu vs B 2.42; sensitivity factors 1.7-25 and 1.8-6.1 vs E, max transformer-row uncoord 0.0231 < 0.025). Limits and disclaimer are unusually candid (constants recalled, swept; coincident heat pumps; TMY; perfect-foresight smart charging). But the headline 'about 18 years to end of life' (README.md:7, also in project.json summary and on the live page) is read from a regime the model and the guide do not support: with the subject's own code, the HP+EV 100% uncoordinated case at loading 0.5 peaks at 2.38 pu and 207 C, spends 49 h above 140 C and 4 h above 180 C, and 92.3% of its annual loss of life comes from those 49 h above 140 C ({S}/ev_indep.py companion one-liner in checks). README.md:42 admits 'the 100 % result is dominated by the overload so its exact figure does not' survive, but the headline and abstract state the end-of-life figure without that caveat beside it. 'Smart charging recovers an EV alone completely' (README.md:7): 0.0026 vs 0.0019 baseline is +40%, immaterial in absolute terms but not 'completely'. The project page abstract says 'at 0.7 per unit every heat-pump case fails', true only for Greensboro (Sand Point HP 100% is 44 %/yr, Miami 0.011). Numbers backed, interpretation of the headline overreaches: 2.
evidence.fitness: A researcher could clone this, reproduce every number in 20 s and swap in sourced constants, which is real value. But the nearest prior work is not cited and the result is not new: Hilshey, Hines, Rezaei and Dowds, 'Estimating the impact of electric vehicle smart charging on distribution transformer aging', IEEE Trans. Smart Grid 4(2), 2013, did the same C57.91 hot-spot/FAA model with ambient temperature and compared uncoordinated against smart EV charging on a residential pole-top transformer; Gong et al., 'Study of PEV charging on residential distribution transformer life', IEEE Trans. Smart Grid 3(1), 2012, likewise; Navarro-Espinosa and Ochoa (IEEE Trans. Power Syst. 2016) and Protopapadaki and Saelens (Applied Energy 2017) assessed heat-pump plus EV impacts on LV networks with realistic diversity. The qualitative finding (smart charging removes EV ageing, coincident heat-pump peaks remain) is consistent with that literature and sound within its assumptions, but the README's 'Builds on' (README.md:9) cites only the standard and the data, so a reader cannot tell what is added. The load model (one diversified BDEW H0 group shape for 10 homes, fully coincident heat pumps with no capacity limit or backup heat, PF 1) and the unsourced constants mean the quantitative thresholds (50 %, 65 %) are not transferable to a real feeder without the next steps. 2.
evidence.domain: Compared against IEEE C57.91 clause 7 and the guide's loading practice. Right: the clause 7 equations (ultimate top-oil rise with R and n, hot-spot gradient with m, exponential top-oil lag, FAA with 15000/383), the 110 C reference at 30 C ambient for 65 C-rise thermally upgraded paper (30 + 80 K = 110), and the 180,000 h life, which is the guide's benchmark from distribution-transformer functional life tests and the appropriate one for this class. Constants (55 K top oil, 25 K gradient, R 3.2, n = m = 0.8, tau 3 h) are within the range I would expect for ONAN distribution units (n = m = 0.8 for ONAN; 80 K hot-spot rise is the 65 C-rise design limit, so 55/25 is the conservative end), but neither I nor the author verified them against the standard; the sensitivity sweep is a reasonable mitigation. Departures a specialist would raise: (a) no check of the hot-spot and top-oil limits the guide uses for loading beyond nameplate; the headline case breaches 140 C for 49 h and 180 C for 4 h, where a planner calls the unit overloaded regardless of LOL; (b) only thermally upgraded insulation (110 C reference); much legacy pole-top stock is 55 C-rise with a 95 C reference (FAA with 15000/368), which would roughly multiply ageing by e^(15000/368-15000/383)= ~4.9 at the same hot spot and is not offered as a parameter; (c) hourly mean load and a diversified German group profile under-represent the 10-service coincident peak; (d) heat pumps without capacity derate or resistance backup, which in a cold snap sets the real peak; (e) PF 1. (a) and (b) are the kind of gaps a planner hits in the first hour: 2.

defects.what: The thermal load functions are tested only at K = 1, where any exponent gives 1: changing the hot-spot gradient K^(2m) to K^m or the top-oil term K^2 R to K R leaves all 8 tests green, as do changes to EV start time, smart availability and the growth multiplier (5 of 7 core mutations survive). No test pins a value at K != 1 (closed form at K=1.5, 30 C: 171.76 C) or a number from results.txt.

Headline 'about 18 years to end of life' (5.6 %/yr, HP+EV 100% uncoordinated, loading 0.5) is computed from a case that peaks at 2.38 pu and 207 C, spends 49 h above 140 C and 4 h above 180 C, with 92% of its annual loss of life from those 49 h; at those hot spots C57.91 loading limits, not cumulative LOL, govern and the model is outside its range. The caveat is at README.md:42 but not beside the headline, in project.json or on the live page.

No prior work cited: Hilshey et al. 2013 (IEEE Trans. Smart Grid, C57.91 ageing under uncoordinated vs smart EV charging), Gong et al. 2012, and the LV heat-pump/EV impact literature (Navarro-Espinosa & Ochoa 2016) cover the same question; the README does not say what is new relative to them.

Only thermally upgraded 65 C-rise insulation (110 C reference, 383 K) is modelled and no hot-spot limit is checked; legacy 55 C-rise pole-top stock uses a 95 C reference (FAA with 368 K, ~4.9x faster ageing at the same hot spot), the case a planner meets first on old streets.

'Smart charging recovers an EV alone completely': 0.0026 vs 0.0019 %/yr baseline is +40% (immaterial in absolute terms); and the project.json/page abstract 'at 0.7 per unit every heat-pump case fails' holds for Greensboro only (Sand Point HP 100% 44 %/yr, Miami 0.011).
Dead code `_plugged` (never called) and unused `from dataclasses import replace`.
Section C header printed into results.txt says 'loading 0.7' while the rows cover loadings 0.5 and 0.7.

verdict: Every number reproduces: a fresh run is byte-identical to results.txt, and an independent C57.91 clause 7 implementation from data/inputs.csv gives Greensboro base 0.001868 and HP-100% 0.3348 %/yr at loading 0.5 (reported 0.00187, 0.334), Sand Point and Miami likewise, EV-100% uncoordinated 0.0355 (0.0354), the 110 C / 85 C rated point, 171.76 C at 1.5 pu, the 6.78 K doubling interval and the 4.87 %/yr rated-life rate. The equations, the 110 C/30 C basis and the 180,000 h distribution-transformer life are applied correctly, and the limits section is candid that the constants are recalled and swept. It does not meet the bar: the tests touch the thermal load function only at K = 1, so 5 of 7 seeded core mutations (including both rise exponents) survive (verification 1); the headline 'about 18 years to end of life' comes from a case with 49 h above 140 C and a 207 C peak, where loading limits rather than loss of life govern (claims 2); and the nearest prior work (Hilshey et al. 2013 and others on EV smart charging and transformer ageing) is not cited, so the result, consistent with that literature, is not placed as new (fitness 2). Finished: everything the README says is done works.
